It is called a veinworm, though nothing about it is soft. On a world whose sky never brightens—no star close enough to matter, only the slow heat of a buried core—light is not a resource. Anything that needs photons starves. The veinworm does not.

It is longer than a person is tall and no thicker than a wrist, a segmented tube of mineral-stiffened hide the color of wet charcoal. Pigment is useless here; the dark is structural, a shell of iron-rich plates grown from the water it drinks. Between the plates the skin is thin and slick, crowded with chemoreceptors so dense they look like frost. It tastes the current the way a fish tastes a river: sulfides, methane, the faint metallic sting of rock just split by quake. Where the chemistry is richest, it slows.

There are no eyes. In their place, a ring of pits around the blunt head reads pressure, heat, and the tiny electric fields of anything that moves in the brine. Farther back, a line of stiff hairs along each flank listens for the groan of stone and the click of other veinworms tapping the same fissure. They do not call. They knock, once, and wait for the echo to come back wrong.

It feeds where the planet leaks. At hydrothermal cracks, bacteria spin energy from chemicals instead of sun, and the veinworm farms them. A gut that runs nearly its whole length is less a stomach than a reactor: folds of tissue keep the microbes warm and fed on seep-water, and in return they leak sugars and amino acids into its blood. It never hunts in the way surface animals do. It finds a seam, anchors with a collar of hooked plates, and drinks the plume until the plume thins. Then it unhooks and follows the taste downhill, toward warmer rock.

Reproduction is a slow argument with scarcity. Two veinworms meet in a fissure only when both have stored enough mineral to spare. They lock head-to-tail, trade packets of cells through a pore behind the sensory ring, and part. Weeks later each sheds a capsule no bigger than a thumbnail, glued to the rock with a glue that hardens into the same iron-dark shell. The young do not swim. They bore, millimeter by millimeter, into the soft edge of the vent field, eating the microbial film as they go, growing plates as the water cools them.

What would kill it is not darkness. Darkness is the medium. What would kill it is a quiet planet: no cracks, no seep, no chemical gradient to follow. CREATURE DESCRIPTION:
It is called a **silt-singer**, and it has never known a photon.

The world it inhabits has no star worth mentioning—or the star is dead, or buried behind a permanent sky of ash and metal vapor. The ground is warm in places, cold in others, and always moving: tectonic sighs, gas vents, slow rivers of mineral slurry under ice that never melts because there is nothing to melt it. Life there runs on chemistry and heat, not sunlight. The silt-singer is one of the things that harvests both.

It is about the length of a human arm and shaped like a flattened teardrop of cartilage and living stone. There is no head in the usual sense. The broad end is a sensory apron: a sheet of skin stretched over a lattice of hollow spines. Those spines are tuned like organ pipes. The creature does not see; it sings a continuous, very low note into the ground and the water, and it reads the world in the way the note comes back—density, tremor, the soft drag of another body moving through silt. Its “eyes” are the places where the return is loudest. Two of them can pass within a hand’s breadth in total dark and know each other’s size, speed, and whether the other has recently fed, because a full gut changes the resonance of the belly.

Color is meaningless to it, but if you could shine a lamp it would look like wet basalt: matte, slightly iridescent only where mineral salts have crusted in the pores. Those pores are not decoration. They drink dissolved metals and vent gases. Along the flanks run rows of chemoreceptive pits, each pit a little cup of mucus that tastes iron, sulfur, ammonia, and the faint sourness of another silt-singer’s trail. It navigates by taste-maps older than any memory. A rich vent smells like a road. A dead vent smells like a closed door.

It has no jaws. The narrow end of the body is a muscular siphon. When it finds a mat of chemosynthetic microbes—pale, heat-loving films that grow where hot water leaks through rock—it presses the siphon down and pulses, drawing the film and the silt beneath it into a gut that is more filter than stomach. The microbes are not plants. They burn hydrogen sulfide and methane the way leaves burn light. The silt-singer burns the microbes. Everything edible on this world is either a chemical engine or something that ate one.

Locomotion is a slow accordion crawl. Rings of muscle contract in waves, gripping with thousands of microscopic hooks made of the same mineral the creature precipitates from the water—calcium, silica, a little iron. The hooks wear down and are regrown constantly. Leave a silt-singer on bare rock and it will polish a shallow oval into the stone over a year, a bed shaped exactly to its body. They sleep in those ovals, if sleep is the word. What they do is drop their song to a murmur and let the ground’s own noise wash through them, the way a person might rest with an ear to a hull.

They are not solitary, but they do not school. A nursery is a warm crack where eggs—translucent capsules no bigger than seeds—are glued to the rock and left. The adults do not guard them. The vent does. Anything that comes to eat the eggs must cross a gradient of heat and poison that the eggs tolerate and most predators do not. When the young hatch they are already singing, tiny and shrill, and they follow the richest chemical thread away from the crack before a larger singer can mistake them for food. Cannibalism is common and not dramatic. In the dark, a body is only another concentration of useful molecules.

What passes for fear is a sudden flattening. The apron spreads, the song jumps an octave, and the body becomes a vibrating disk that is hard to bite and easy to lose in the slurry. What passes for courtship is two songs locking into a chord that neither could make alone, held for hours while they lie parallel in a trench, tasting each other’s flanks, deciding whether the chord is stable enough to justify the cost of eggs. If it breaks, they part without damage. If it holds, they glue a clutch and separate. Pair-bonds would be a luxury. Vents die. Continents of ice shift. A partner you cannot find again is not a partner.

There is no bioluminescence worth the energy. Light would advertise a meal to anything that could use it, and nothing here can. The closest they come to ornament is sound. An old silt-singer’s song is lower and slower, complicated with overtones that younger ones cannot yet produce. In the deep trenches where the rock is thick and the echo carries for kilometers, those old songs layer over each other into something that is not language and not music, but is unmistakably shared: a map of which vents are failing, which are new, where the ice has cracked. A newcomer can cross a continent it has never touched and arrive at food, guided only by the leftovers of other voices in the stone.

If you stood on that world and turned on a lamp, the silt-singer would not flinch from the brightness—it has no receptors for it. It would flinch from the heat of the bulb, and from the tiny vibration of your pulse through your boots. Then it would taste the metal of the lamp, decide you were neither vent nor meat worth the risk, and sink back into the silt, song dimming to a thread.

The dark would close. It would never have noticed the light.

- **Chemistry.** Pores along the plate taste the air for sulfides, ammonia, and the sharp signature of rotting organic matter—or of another vell.

The only heat is leftover from the world’s birth, leaking up through cracks in a crust of frozen nitrogen and iron grit. The thrum lives in those cracks, where the temperature rises just enough for a thin film of ammonia-rich slurry to stay liquid.

Its body is a flattened ribbon of cartilage and gel, about as long as a human arm and no thicker than a wrist. There is no front and no back in any permanent sense. The ribbon can thicken at either end, split into two blunt lobes, or coil into a tight spiral when the rock shifts. Skin is not skin but a mat of mineral-laced fibers that stiffen or soften with temperature. In the coldest reaches it goes rigid as wire; nearer a vent it becomes slick and almost liquid, able to pour itself through a fissure narrower than a finger.

It does not see, hear, or smell in any way we would recognize. The entire surface is a pressure organ. Every grain of grit that brushes it, every faint tremor in the stone, every slight change in the density of the slurry registers as a pattern across that skin. A thrum can tell the difference between a settling pebble and the footfall of another of its kind from several body-lengths away. It navigates by the geometry of vibration the way a bat navigates by echoes, except the “sound” is the planet itself creaking.

Feeding is slow and chemical. Along both edges of the ribbon run rows of pores that weep a weak acid, dissolving trace metals and simple organics locked in the rock. The dissolved slurry is drawn inward through channels no wider than a hair and metabolized by colonies of microbes the thrum carries in internal pockets. Those microbes are as much a part of it as its cartilage. When food is scarce, the thrum slows until its pulse—a sluggish contraction that travels the length of the ribbon once every few hours—nearly stops. It can remain in that near-stillness for years.

Reproduction is a matter of division under stress. If a vent cools or a passage collapses, the ribbon pinches at its middle and the two halves separate. Each half already contains a full set of the microbial partners and enough stored minerals to regrow the missing length. There is no mating, no courtship, no sex. The only social behavior is avoidance: two thrums that meet will each shift their pulse rhythm until the interference pattern tells them which way the other is moving, and then they drift apart. Crowding means shared food, and food is already almost nothing.

Color is meaningless here, but if a light were somehow brought to it, the thrum would look dull gray-brown, the color of wet slate, with paler streaks where mineral deposits have crusted along old scars. It would not react to the light. Light is not a stimulus it has any receptor for. It would only notice the heat of the lamp, and it would recoil from that the way we recoil from a burn, folding itself into the coldest shadow it can find until the strange warmth passed.

It never learned the idea of brightness. On a world sealed under permanent cloud and ice, light is not scarce so much as irrelevant—an unused medium, like a color no eye was built to see. The creature that fills that vacancy is called, by the people who study it, a **nullwalker**.

It is longer than a person is tall, low and flexible, with a body shaped more like a drifting ribbon than a beast. Its skin is the color of wet basalt and slightly cooler than the rock it presses against. There are no eyes, not even buried ones. Where a face might be, the skull is smooth and blunt, perforated by two deep spirals that open and close with each slow breath. Those spirals do not smell in the way ours do. They sample pressure, mineral dust, and the faint electrical taste of moving water.

The nullwalker navigates by the planet’s own mutter. Every footfall, every shift of ice, every trickle under the crust sends a tremor through the ground. Along its underside runs a double row of pale, cartilage-tipped nodes. They press into stone and read the returning echo the way a fingertip reads a page. A distant rockslide is a long, low chord. A nearer creature is a sharper knock. From those differences it builds a map that is always a few heartbeats behind the present and never wrong about distance.

Heat is its other sense. The world has hot seams—thin veins of geothermal water threading black stone. The nullwalker’s flanks carry shallow pits lined with living crystal that swell or tighten as temperature changes by a fraction of a degree. It follows those seams the way a river follows a slope, grazing on mats of chemosynthetic film that grow where mineral-rich water meets cold rock. It does not hunt often. When it must, it waits beside a seam until something smaller comes to feed, then folds its body over the spot and pins the prey with a sudden, silent contraction. There is no flash, no cry that travels far. Sound here is too useful to waste.

Its blood is thick and dark, loaded with compounds that keep tissues flexible near freezing. On a world wrapped in permanent black—an airless crust over a warm, chemically restless ocean, where the only sky is rock and the only “day” is the slow pulse of the planet’s heat—it has never needed eyes, and it has never grown any.

Its body is a long, flexible ribbon of pale tissue, about the length of a human arm when it is relaxed and nearly twice that when it stretches to hunt. The skin is not smooth. It is a field of microscopic hairs and fluid-filled pits, each one a sensor. Pressure, temperature, the faintest chemical gradient, the tremor of something else moving through the water—all of that arrives as texture against its flanks. What we would call darkness is, for it, a crowded room of currents and tastes.

Along its underside run two rows of gill-slits that do not breathe oxygen the way fish do. They filter dissolved minerals and the waste of chemosynthetic microbes that bloom around cracks in the seafloor. The hush-gill does not chase light-fed plankton. It grazes the bacterial mats that form where hot water seeps from the rock, and when those mats thin, it follows the chemical plume upstream the way a moth follows a scent, except the plume is sulfur, methane, and iron, and the “trail” is a gradient only a few molecules thick.

Its mouth is a soft, circular hood ringed with retractable filaments. The filaments are not teeth. They are tongues and fingers at once: they taste a surface, decide if it is edible, and if it is, they grip and tear in slow, patient pulls. Digestion is slow. A good meal of bacterial crust can last it for days, which matters, because food is patchy and the water is cold away from the vents.

It does not glow. Light would be wasted here, and anything bright enough to see by would also advertise it to whatever else is listening. Instead it is almost perfectly still when it is not feeding. Its color, if a lamp were somehow brought down, would be a dull, bloodless gray—pigment is expensive when nothing ever sees you—and its blood, if it has something we would call blood, runs thick with compounds that bind the poisons of the vent water and turn them into fuel.

Reproduction is a quiet business. When two hush-gills meet in a mineral-rich eddy, they press their flanks together and trade packets of cells through temporary pores. There is no display, no chase. Afterward each one carries a clutch of embryos in a fold along its back until the young are large enough to filter for themselves. The parent does not guard them. In a world without vision, presence is already a risk; better to scatter and trust the chemistry.

What it fears are not shadows—there are no shadows—but sudden changes in taste: the metallic tang of a larger scavenger’s wake, the sour bloom of a vent that is dying, the flat emptiness of water that has not touched rock in a long time. When that happens it flattens against the seafloor, matches the local current, and waits. Waiting is its oldest skill. The creature is called a **vell**, and it has never seen anything, because nothing on its world can be seen.

Its planet, **Nerath**, orbits a dead star. The sky is not dark the way a cloudy night is dark. It is a total absence: no sun, no reflected moons, no bioluminescent seas. Heat still leaks from the planet’s core and from chemical reactions in the crust, so life exists, but it exists entirely outside vision.

### Body

A vell is about the size of a wolf and shaped more like a flattened, jointless question mark. Its skin is pale, almost translucent, and permanently damp—a thin film of mucus that conducts chemical signals and keeps sensory organs from drying in the thin, cold air. There are no eyes, not even vestigial pits. The skull is a smooth dome of cartilage. Where a face might be, the skin folds into a wide, soft muzzle ringed with hundreds of hair-fine chemoreceptors, each tuned to a different class of molecule: metal ions, sulfur compounds, the sweet rot of geothermal mats, the sharp signature of another vell’s fear.

Along both flanks run lateral lines of pressure organs, like a fish’s, but denser. They read the planet’s constant low wind, the shudder of distant ice cracking, and the footfalls of anything heavier than a pebble within roughly thirty meters. A vell “maps” its world as a shifting field of pressure and scent, updated several times a second.

### How it moves

It does not walk so much as flow. Six short, muscular pads grip the rock; between them, the belly can inflate and deflate, letting the animal hover a finger’s width above the ground on a cushion of exhaled air when the surface is treacherous. On stable ground it prefers contact. Traction matters more than speed. Nerath’s surface is a maze of mineral crusts, brine seeps, and sudden vents. Running blind into a vent is death. The vell’s gait is deliberate: three pads always planted, body low, head sweeping side to side so the chemoreceptors sample a wide arc.

When it must cross open ground, it drums. A hardened plate under the throat taps the rock in short patterns. Echoes return through the lateral lines. The resolution is crude—boulder, hollow, drop, living mass—but enough to keep it from walking off a shelf.

Plants, in any ordinary sense, do not exist. The base of the food web is microbial mats fed by chemical energy: hydrogen, methane, reduced iron, sulfur. The vell grazes these mats and also hunts the small, wormlike animals that graze them more efficiently. Its mouth is a circular, muscular ring lined with backward-facing keratin hooks. It does not bite so much as inhale and clamp. Digestion is slow and hot; a vell’s core runs several degrees warmer than the air, and it spends long periods pressed flat against warm rock, dumping excess heat or soaking it up depending on the vent season.

It can go weeks without a large meal. When it does feed well, it caches. Not by burying—burial is hard to relocate without sight—but by smearing a unique blend of glandular oils on the site. Those oils persist for months and are readable only at close range, a private map written in smell.

Electric fields matter. Many of Nerath’s small animals generate weak bioelectric pulses as they move through conductive brine. The vell’s muzzle can detect those pulses at short range, the way a shark detects a struggling fish. It also carries a crude magnetic sense in iron-rich crystals embedded near the brain, oriented to the planet’s field. That sense does not give it a compass rose it can “see.” It gives it a feeling of alignment: this way is downslope toward the great rift; that way is back toward the home seep. Lost vells walk in widening spirals until the magnetic feeling and a familiar chemical front coincide.

Hearing is excellent in the low frequencies. High squeaks die quickly in the dense, cold air and are nearly useless. The vell’s world is thumps, groans, and the long drone of wind over ridges.

### Social life

Vells are not solitary, but their company is mostly chemical. A group shares a seep and maintains a boundary of scent posts—glandular marks on prominent rocks—that say who is present, who is breeding, who is injured. They rarely touch except to mate or to huddle for heat during a cold pulse, when surface temperatures crash after a vent field goes quiet. Huddled, they synchronize breathing. The shared rhythm makes the group’s pressure-signature distinct, so a returning vell can find the pile in the dark without stumbling into it.

Conflict is mostly display. A threatened vell inflates its flank sacs and releases a bitter aerosol. The rival reads the concentration and either yields or answers with a stronger plume. Physical fights happen, but they are expensive: a torn chemoreceptor can mean weeks of hunger. Most disputes end when one animal’s scent simply goes faint as it retreats upwind.

Eggs are leathery and laid in warm cracks, then sealed with mucus that both hides the chemical trace and keeps the eggs from drying. Hatchlings emerge already eyeless, already smelling. The first thing a newborn does is press its muzzle to the mother’s flank and memorize her oil. That signature is home. If the seep dies, the mother leads the young by laying a trail of the same oil, refreshed every few body-lengths, a breadcrumb path through a world that offers no landmarks a human would recognize.

There is no darkness in the vell’s experience, because darkness is a visual idea. There is near and far, warm and cold, familiar and foreign, safe pressure and the sharp chemical edge of a predator’s breath. Its mind is a layered model of gradients. Beauty, if the word applies, is a clean seep: rich iron, steady warmth, no foreign oils, the low comfortable thrum of the group breathing in the same rhythm. Danger is a sudden stillness in the pressure field, followed by a smell that does not belong to anything that grazes mats.

It will never know that other worlds have light. It does not miss it. On Nerath, light would be a useless extra, and eyes would be soft tissue waiting to freeze. The vell is not incomplete. It is built exactly for the planet it has.

CREATURE DESCRIPTION:
It is called a hollow-singer, and it has never known a shadow.

The creature is long and low, a little under the length of a human arm if you include the trailing feelers, and it moves the way a hand moves under a blanket: not by stepping so much as by pulling the world toward itself. Its body is a soft, segmented tube, pale as wet bone only because there is nothing to stain it. Pigment would be wasted. Skin is thin enough that the pulse shows through as a slow dimpling, and the whole surface is studded with pressure pits—tiny cups that read the weight of air the way eyes read a room. A footfall two body-lengths away arrives as a map: direction, mass, whether the thing is crawling or settling.

Where a face might be, there is a ring. Six boneless arms rise from it, each no thicker than a finger, each ending in a fan of hairs so fine they stir when something breathes. The hollow-singer does not see with them. It tastes distance. Minerals leached into the still air, the sweet rot of a fungal mat, the metallic note of another creature’s blood-wet mouth—all of it is sorted in the ring and passed inward. The mouth itself is not a bite so much as a sleeve. It everts, soft and ridged, and draws food in by a ripple, the way a throat swallows. Teeth would be loud. Loud is a mistake.

Along the belly runs a double row of sucker-pads, and between them a groove that never quite closes. That groove is the instrument. When the hollow-singer is alone, it keeps the groove shut and moves in silence, pads lifting one after another so the body never fully leaves the stone. When it must speak—mating, warning, the slow census of who else is in the cavern—it opens the groove a fraction and drives air across a ribbed membrane. The sound is not a cry. It is a low, shaped hush, pitched below what most surface ears would call hearing, and it travels through rock better than through air. Other hollow-singers answer in kind. A chorus, if you could stand in that dark and wait, would feel like the cave itself remembering a melody.

It has no eyes, and the skull—if the cartilaginous hood at the front counts as one—has no sockets where eyes could have been. The ancestors lost them so completely that the nerves were borrowed for something else: a lattice under the hood that reads faint electric fields. In waterless dark, on dry stone, the field is weak, but living muscle still leaks a little current. A prey-thing the size of a thumb registers as a soft tug, a direction without an image. The hollow-singer turns toward it the way a plant turns toward warmth, unhurried, already sure.

Heat is its other compass. A strip of tissue along each flank is dense with vessels held just under the skin, and the creature can flush or drain them to match the stone. Most of the time it is exactly as warm as the ground, which is to say cold, and a hunter that stalks by warmth walks over it and feels only rock. When it must move fast it pays for it: the flank-strips warm, the outline blooms, and for a little while it is visible to anything that hunts the way it hunts. So it rarely hurries. Patience is the local law.

Reproduction is a duet. Two hollow-singers find each other by the hush-note and lie parallel, grooves open, exchanging a mucus thread that carries packets of cells. There is no nest in the open. The thread is pressed into a crack, sealed with a paste of saliva and mineral dust, and left. The young hatch already armed with pressure pits and a working groove, thumb-sized, and they sing a thinner version of the adult note so their parents—if “parent” is the right word for a creature that may never meet them—can avoid crushing them in the dark. Most are eaten anyway, by kin or by the slow, blind grazers that crop the fungal mats. The cavern does not keep extras.

What it eats is whatever the mats do not finish: shed casings, the soft eggs of smaller tunnelers, the occasional carcass that has gone quiet. It is not a chaser. It is a listener that arrives after the struggle is over, sleeve-mouth working, arms tasting the edges to be sure nothing is still twitching. Waste is deposited in the same cracks the young are not using, and the fungi take it back. Nothing here is thrown away, because nothing here can afford a trail.

If you brought a light, the hollow-singer would not understand it as light. The sudden warmth of a lamp would read as a body; the click of a switch as a footfall with no weight behind it. It would freeze, flank-strips drained, groove shut, and become a ridge in the stone until the strange heat moved on. Only if you stayed, breathing, shifting your mass, would the pressure pits draw the outline of you—tall, loud, leaking heat from every inch—and the hollow-singer would ease backward into a crack narrower than its body looks capable of entering, arms folded, song held in its throat.

On that planet the dark is not an absence the creature endures. It is the medium, as water is to a fish. Color, glare, the whole theater of seeing: none of it was ever offered, so none of it is missed. What the hollow-singer has instead is a world made of pressure, taste, hush, and the faint electric rumor of other lives, and it moves through that world as completely as anything that has ever opened its eyes.
